title: Differentiation Is Darn Difficult
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos, a reading specialist, uses her own history as a parent and teacher to argue that differentiating instruction in classrooms with vast ranges of ability is more often pondered than done well. Her sons sat at opposite ends of the reading continuum, and most of their early teachers, like her, did not know how to teach beginning reading. From her kindergarten teaching she concludes that foundational phonics instruction for students who depend on it must take precedence, even when high achievers are already past those skills. She asks parents and critics to extend grace to teachers handling an enormous spread of skills, while still insisting on better training in the science of reading. The essay is personal and warm, with data on third-grade reading and Black boys quoted from another writer.
points: Only a minority of children learn to read regardless of instruction; most need explicit, systematic teaching, as her younger son did.
In a class with a vast range of abilities, she prioritises the students who need her most while accommodating the rest as best she can.
Foundational skills essential for most students, such as encoding before decoding and phonemic awareness with letters, were unnecessary for early readers, which shows the tension in differentiation.
Teacher training in beginning reading remains a gap, and parents should extend grace to teachers managing wide skill ranges.
Realistic differentiation must be pedagogically possible and humanly possible.
quotes: Of course we need to address the needs of all of our students—which is not just a cliché that we robotically recite but a goal we actually value. However, the question of how to effectively differentiate instruction when the range of abilities in a class is not just vast but often vastly unmanageable, is a question more easily pondered than responded to.

It is a minority of children like me and my older son who learn to read regardless of instruction. Far more common are the experiences of my younger son who greatly benefited from his first grade teacher’s systematic phonics instruction.

The truth is that I didn’t need to be hard on their teachers. They didn’t know better (and, for that matter, neither did I), so they did what they thought was best, even if it was a far cry from what many of their students needed.

But I also know that my high expectations for myself often go unrealized, which is why I always prioritize those students who need me most, while simultaneously attempting to accommodate the rest of the class to the best of my ability. If I don’t prioritize the needs of my most vulnerable students, they run the risk of falling behind and never catching up.

If we could, we would differentiate instruction through the kind of individualized attention I was able to provide by happenstance, but we know this simply isn’t realistic within the structure of our teaching day in most of our public school classrooms, so we make do with the time we have and the opportunities we can snatch from the jaws of the timetable.
Please, parents, understand that not all kids are alright—not by a long way—but chances are your high-achievers will be.

All we can do is extend grace when our grandiose expectations fall flat for both. Forgiveness means giving up all hope for a better past (who can we credit for that great line?), so let’s just work on a better future within the realm of what’s pedagogically possible—yes—but also humanly possible.
